Let quadratic function \(f\) be defined below:

\[f(x)~=~x^{2}+{6}x-{207}\]

When curve \(y=f(x)\) is graphed, we see two \(x\)-intercepts at \((x_1,0)\) and \((x_2,0)\).


In exact form, those \(x\) intercepts can be expressed as \(h\pm p\sqrt{q}\).

\[x_1=h-p\sqrt{q}\] \[x_2=h+p\sqrt{q}\]

Find the values of \(h\), \(p\), and \(q\).

\(h=\)

\(p=\)

\(q=\)

The \(x\) intercepts occur when either \(x_1\) or \(x_2\) satisfies \(f(x)=0\).

\[x^{2}+{6}x-{207}=0\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=1\] \[b=6\] \[c=-207\]

Plug numbers into the quadratic formula!

\[x = \frac{-(6)\pm\sqrt{(6)^2-4(1)(-207)}}{2(1)} \]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{36-(-828)}}{2}\]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{864}}{2}\]

Use prime factorization.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot3\cdot3}}{2}\]

Isolate the twin factors.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot3}\cdot \sqrt{2\cdot3}}{2}\]

Simplify the square root of the square.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm 2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot \sqrt{2\cdot3}}{2}\]

Simplify the integer products.

\[x = \frac{-6 \pm 12\cdot \sqrt{6}}{2}\]

Split the fraction.

\[x = \frac{-6}{2} \pm \frac{12\cdot \sqrt{6}}{2}\]

Both numerators contain a factor of 2.

\[x = -3 \pm 6\sqrt{6}\]

So, \(h=-3\) and \(p=6\) and \(q=6\).

I should mention this means we could now write the function in factored form.

\[f(x)~=~\left[x-(-3-6\sqrt{6})\right]\cdot\left[x-(-3+6\sqrt{6})\right]\]

A quadratic function, \(f\), has zeros at \((x_1,0)\) and \((x_2,0)\).


The exact zeros are \(2\pm 3\sqrt{2}\).

\[x_1~=~2-3\sqrt{2}\] \[x_2~=~2+3\sqrt{2}\]

The function \(f\) can be expressed in factored form, with parameter \(a\) adjusting the vertical stretch and orientation of the parabola.

\[f(x)~=~a\cdot \left[x-(2-3\sqrt{2})\right]\cdot\left[x-(2+3\sqrt{2})\right]\]

The function, expressed in standard form, is parameterized with quadratic coefficient \(a\), linear coefficient \(b\), and constant \(c\).

\[f(x)~=~ax^2+bx+c\]

In this case, the quadratic coefficient equals 1.

\[a=1\]

Find the linear coefficient and the constant. You can do this by expanding the factored form and combining like terms.

\(b=\)

\(c=\)

Start in factored form. We know \(a=1\).

\[f(x)~=~\left[x-(2-3\sqrt{2})\right]\cdot\left[x-(2+3\sqrt{2})\right]\]

At this point, you can either FOIL or distribute away the inside parentheses. I think it'll be a bit cleaner to distribute the subtraction across the parentheses.

\[\left[x-2+3\sqrt{2}\right]\cdot\left[x-2-3\sqrt{2}\right]\]

But now, instead of FOIL, we need to generalize, because each factor has three terms: a linear term and two constant terms. You could probably guess that we simply multiply each of the first factor's terms by each of the second factor's terms.

\[x^2-2x-3\sqrt{2}x-2x+4+6\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{2}x-6\sqrt{2}-18\]

Combine like terms. Opposite terms cancel each other out.

\[x^2-4x-14\]

Thus, \(b=-4\) and \(c=-14\).

A quadratic function, \(f\), has zeros at \((x_1,0)\) and \((x_2,0)\).
